newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Dunne questions Morgan's campaign spending.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Dunne questions Morgan's campaign spending.

text.p: United New Zealand Party leader Peter Dunne on Thursday called for an investigation of New Zealand First MP Tukoroirangi Morgan's election expenditure declaration which included expenses for buying meat.

"Section 217 (2)(b) of the Electoral Act specifically excludes candidates from providing food or drink for the purposes ... of procuring himself or herself to be elected ..." Dunne said in a press statement.
"Mr Morgan clearly bought food to be provided to potential voters as he had declared so to the Electoral Commission," Dunne said.

"The penalty for breaching this part of the Act, known as Corrupt and Illegal Pracices' with the accompanying appropriate High Court actions would require Mr Morgan's resignation from Parliament," Dunne said.
Section 217 states "the provision of a light supper after an election meeting shall be deemed not to constitute the offence of treating".
Dunne said he would call on the Electoral Commissioner to investigate.
But Electoral Commissioner Paul Harris said the returns were a matter for the Chief Electoral Office and he had informed Dunne's office of this.
"It's the chief electoral office and returning officers who are responsible for candidates' returns of election expenses, not us," Harris told Reuters.
According to media reports, Morgan declared expenditure including $160 for a pig, $200 spent at the "Mad Butcher" and $39.30 for smoked bacon bones.

Morgan is already under pressure from opposition MPs to resign after revelations he spent more than $4000 on clothes at the expense of Maori language television station Aotearoa Television only weeks before he was elected to Parliament.
If Morgan were to resign the government's slim majority in the House would be threatened.

The National-New Zealand First coalition controls 61 seats in the 120 seat House. But free-market Act New Zealand, with eight seats and United's Dunne would be likely to support a continuation of centre-right government.
A spokesman for Prime Minister Jim Bolger, Richard Griffin, said the government was not taking the matter seriously.
"Our official view is that Peter Dunne has a very good sense of humour," Griffin said.
